items.stem: Which of the following best describes "iambic pentameter"?
options: A line of five iambs (unstressed–stressed pairs), ten syllables, common in English verse
A poem in which a single persona speaks to a silent listener, revealing their character
The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse
items.answer: A line of five iambs (unstressed–stressed pairs), ten syllables, common in English verse

items.stem: Explain why a poet might choose a strict form for a poem about chaos or loss.
items.answer: The tension between ordered form and disordered content can suggest an attempt to control grief, or make the breakdown more striking.

items.stem: Distinguish between blank verse and free verse.
items.answer: Free verse has no regular metre or rhyme; blank verse is unrhymed but written in regular iambic pentameter.
items.markingKey: Free verse has no regular metre or rhyme; blank verse is unrhymed but written in regular iambic pentameter. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Free verse is poetry with no structure." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Free verse lacks regular metre and rhyme but uses deliberate structure – line breaks, stanza shapes, repetition – for effect.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'Suitcase' (an original poem written for study).

Suitcase

My mother packed the country in a suitcase:
two spoons, one photograph, a jar of soil
that customs took. She did not argue.
She had already lost the bigger things.

Now she waters basil on a London sill
and talks to it in a language
the neighbours think is weather.

Explain the effect of the poem's stanza form, line length or rhyme.
items.answer: Free verse in two stanzas, a quatrain and a tercet; the stanza break marks the shift from past departure to present life, and enjambment ("a jar of soil / that customs took") delays the loss.
items.markingKey: Free verse in two stanzas, a quatrain and a tercet; the stanza break marks the shift from past departure to present life, and enjambment ("a jar of soil / that customs took") delays the loss. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following opening lines of Wilfred Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est' (written 1917, published 1920).

Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.

Analyse the poet's structural choices in this poem.
items.answer: The lines are in roughly iambic pentameter with alternate rhyme (ABAB), but the rhythm is broken by heavy stresses and caesuras, enacting the soldiers' exhaustion.
items.markingKey: The lines are in roughly iambic pentameter with alternate rhyme (ABAB), but the rhythm is broken by heavy stresses and caesuras, enacting the soldiers' exhaustion. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Form is the most important element of a poem's meaning."
items.answer: Form is integral rather than supreme: it matters most when it interacts with imagery and voice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: form shapes rhythm, emphasis and expectation; a change of form can signal a change of meaning. Arguments against: imagery and voice carry much of the meaning; many readers respond first to language. items.stem:
Read the following poem 'The Statue Speaks' (an original poem written for study).

The Statue Speaks

They raised me in the square in 1889
and gave me a sword I never held in life.
Each spring the children climb me for photographs.
Each autumn someone paints my hands red.
I do not mind. I was a merchant, mostly.
The war they carved me for was mostly other people's.

How does the poet use sound to reinforce meaning?
items.answer: The flat rhythm and repetition of "mostly" create deadpan irony.
items.markingKey: The flat rhythm and repetition of "mostly" create deadpan irony. items.stem:
Read the following poem 'For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios' (an original poem written for study).

For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios

His hands knew static the way a farmer knows rain:
patient, listening for the voice inside the noise.
The day he died, I turned the dial
through every station in the city,
and every one was speaking,
and none of them was him.

Analyse the imagery in this poem.
items.answer: The simile "the way a farmer knows rain" gives the grandfather's skill patience and closeness to nature; "the voice inside the noise" is a metaphor for finding meaning – and for the speaker's search for him.
items.markingKey: The simile "the way a farmer knows rain" gives the grandfather's skill patience and closeness to nature; "the voice inside the noise" is a metaphor for finding meaning – and for the speaker's search for him. items.stem: Explain the difference between assonance and alliteration.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter

She learned the sea before her name,
the way it hushed, the way it roared;
she learned that light is not a flame
but something patient, kept, restored.

Now ships go by on satellite,
the tower's lamp is switched by phone;
she climbs the stairs most nights to light
a dark that no one calls her own.

items.stem: "Free verse is poetry with no structure." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Free verse lacks regular metre and rhyme but uses deliberate structure – line breaks, stanza shapes, repetition – for effect.
items.markingKey: Free verse lacks regular metre and rhyme but uses deliberate structure – line breaks, stanza shapes, repetition – for effect. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following opening lines of Wilfred Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est' (written 1917, published 1920).

Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.

Analyse how sound patterning contributes to the poem's effect.
items.answer: Harsh consonants ("Knock-kneed", "coughing", "cursed") and the slow "trudge" create a heavy, painful sound.
items.markingKey: Harsh consonants ("Knock-kneed", "coughing", "cursed") and the slow "trudge" create a heavy, painful sound. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter' (an original poem written for study).

The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter

She learned the sea before her name,
the way it hushed, the way it roared;
she learned that light is not a flame
but something patient, kept, restored.

Now ships go by on satellite,
the tower's lamp is switched by phone;
she climbs the stairs most nights to light
a dark that no one calls her own.

Describe the speaker of the poem and their attitude to the subject.
items.answer: A third-person speaker observes the daughter with sympathy; the tone moves from reverent to elegiac.
items.markingKey: A third-person speaker observes the daughter with sympathy; the tone moves from reverent to elegiac. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: A student claims: "A good analytical paragraph mentions as many devices as possible." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Depth matters more than breadth: developing one or two well-chosen features fully earns more credit than listing many.
items.markingKey: Depth matters more than breadth: developing one or two well-chosen features fully earns more credit than listing many. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Form is the most important element of a poem's meaning."
items.answer: Form is integral rather than supreme: it matters most when it interacts with imagery and voice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: form shapes rhythm, emphasis and expectation; a change of form can signal a change of meaning. Arguments against: imagery and voice carry much of the meaning; many readers respond first to language. Supported judgement: Form is integral rather than supreme: it matters most when it interacts with imagery and voice.

items.stem: "Sound is less important than imagery in poetry read silently." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Sound remains important; poems are written for the ear, and silent reading still registers rhythm and sound.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: silent reading emphasises meaning and image; readers often notice imagery first. Arguments against: readers "hear" poems internally; sound shapes pace and mood even in silence. items.stem: "Dramatic monologue is the most effective way for poetry to explore marginalised perspectives." Discuss.
items.answer: It is powerful but not unique, and its ethics depend on who speaks for whom.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives a voice directly; irony can reveal more than the speaker knows. Arguments against: lyric and narrative poems also do this; a poet ventriloquising others raises questions of appropriation.
